analysis.one_liner: Requires taxis and ride-hail services to provide wheelchair-accessible vehicles for disabled riders.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors in the final weeks of the session and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require taxi companies, for-hire transportation companies, and ride-hail services to make accessible vehicles available to people with disabilities and to stop practices like charging extra for an accessible ride or refusing service animals. It would also run national design competitions for a low-cost accessible taxi and an accessible car that drivers can enter from their wheelchairs, create a federal board to track accessible-vehicle availability, require states to write plans for expanding accessible transportation, set federal accessibility standards, and give small taxi companies a tax credit for buying or converting accessible vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities — especially wheelchair users — who today often cannot get a taxi or ride-hail trip at all, wait far longer for an accessible vehicle, or face surcharges and refusals. Small taxi companies would get a tax credit to help cover the cost of accessible vehicles.

how_it_helps.text: Requires owners and operators of for-hire transportation companies, taxi services, and transportation network companies to provide or arrange adequate accessible vehicles for riders with disabilities.

Bars discriminatory treatment, including denying full and equal access to transportation, imposing surcharges for accessible taxis, and refusing service animals, with the enforcement remedies of the Americans with Disabilities Act available to aggrieved riders.

Directs the Federal Transit Administration to hold national competitions to design an accessible taxi that costs no more than a minivan to build and an accessible passenger car that can be sold for no more than 75% of the average new-car price.

Creates an Accessible Taxi and For-Hire Transportation Board, requires annual federal reporting on the availability of accessible vehicles nationwide, and requires every state to develop a strategic plan to expand accessible for-hire transportation.

Requires federal accessibility and service standards, including comparable wait times for accessible vehicles, and gives small taxi companies a tax credit for purchasing or adapting an accessible taxi vehicle.

analysis.who_pays: Taxi, limousine, and ride-hail companies bear the cost of buying and operating accessible vehicles and meeting service standards; taxpayers fund the design competition prizes and the new board; states must write and submit plans. The bill offsets some cost for small taxi companies through the tax credit.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small taxi fleets, which would need to buy or convert wheelchair-accessible vehicles; the bill only partially offsets this with a tax credit limited to small businesses that are qualified taxi companies.
The competitions, the nine-member board, annual reporting, and state strategic plans add new federal and state administrative work with costs authorized but not specified.

Service standards requiring comparable wait times would be difficult to enforce in a market where accessible vehicles are scarce, and the bill does not directly fund vehicle purchases beyond the small-business tax credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — disabled riders being able to get a ride at all — is large for a group the Americans with Disabilities Act has never fully covered in this segment of transportation. The costs are real but moderate: vehicle compliance for operators, taxpayer-funded prizes, and administrative planning. The main weakness is that the bill leans on mandates and planning rather than direct funding, so operators with thin margins might resist compliance even if the bill had become law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in the last weeks of the session and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, less than four months before the 113th Congress ended.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it received no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxi, limousine, and ride-hail companies are better off because the bill died: they avoid a requirement to provide accessible vehicles and the cost that comes with it. Riders with disabilities gained nothing and remain without a federal guarantee of accessible for-hire transportation.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: Senator from Iowa; author of the Americans with Disabilities Act
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; took no further recorded action before retiring at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 18, 2014 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party-line fight; a lone Democrat introduced it, no members of either party signed on, and no roll-call votes were taken.

industries.note: The bill requires taxi fleets to provide accessible vehicles and meet service standards, a real cost, but gives small licensed taxi companies a tax credit for buying or adapting accessible vehicles. Their resistance centers on vehicle cost, while the benefit — rides for disabled passengers — flows to the public.

Uber-style network companies are explicitly covered and would have to arrange adequate accessible vehicles and comply with the nondiscrimination rules, including the ban on surcharges for accessible rides. No offsetting credit is provided for them.

The bill creates voluntary cash-prize competitions for designing a low-cost accessible taxi and an accessible passenger car, opening a potential new market without mandating anything. Participation is optional.
